knownIssues.title: Air conditioning refrigerant loss and compressor wear
knownIssues.description: Weak, intermittent or absent cooling is common on this generation, usually caused by a slow refrigerant leak at hose fittings or the condenser, or by a worn/seized compressor. It typically appears from around 90,000 km onward, is more noticeable in summer, and does not affect drivability but reduces cabin comfort.

fixes.summary: Recharge refrigerant and seal a leak
fixes.steps: 1) Confirm the diagnosis with a manifold gauge set to check refrigerant pressure and a UV dye/electronic leak detector to locate the leak. 2) Tools/parts: manifold gauge set, UV dye or electronic sniffer, replacement refrigerant (R134a), vacuum pump. 3) Vacuum the A/C circuit to remove air and moisture, seal or replace the leaking fitting/hose, then recharge to the specified refrigerant weight from the underbonnet label. 4) Verify by running the A/C for 15-20 minutes and confirming stable low/high side pressures and vent temperature below 10°C. 5) If the leak is inside the condenser core or evaporator, escalate to a workshop with A/C recovery equipment rather than attempting it as a driveway DIY job.

fixes.summary: Replace a seized or noisy A/C compressor
fixes.steps: 1) Confirm diagnosis: a compressor that is noisy, seized, or not engaging the clutch when A/C is requested, verified with an A/C system scan or manual clutch check. 2) Tools/parts: replacement compressor, receiver-drier, refrigerant, vacuum pump, torque wrench. 3) Recover the existing refrigerant, remove the drive belt, disconnect the refrigerant lines, replace the compressor and receiver-drier, then evacuate the system to remove moisture. 4) Recharge with the correct refrigerant and oil quantities and verify stable pressures and cold air at the vents. 5) This job requires refrigerant recovery/handling equipment - have it done at a workshop rather than releasing refrigerant to atmosphere.

fixes.summary: Clean or replace a blocked condenser
fixes.steps: 1) Confirm diagnosis: reduced cooling with high head pressure and visible debris or bent fins on the condenser (in front of the radiator). 2) Tools/parts: soft brush or low-pressure air/water, fin comb, replacement condenser and O-rings if damaged. 3) Remove the front bumper cover for access, clean the condenser fins or replace the unit if leaking or badly damaged, then reconnect and evacuate/recharge the circuit. 4) Verify by checking head pressure returns to normal range and airflow through the fins is unobstructed. 5) Escalate to a workshop if replacement requires refrigerant recovery equipment you do not have.

knownIssues.title: Ignition coil pack failure causing misfires
knownIssues.description: Ignition coils on this 1.2 TSI engine family can fail intermittently, producing a rough idle, hesitation under load and an illuminated engine warning light due to misfires. It is more common in damp or cold weather and typically appears from around 100,000 km, and while not a safety issue, prolonged driving with a misfire can damage the catalytic converter.

fixes.steps: 1) Confirm diagnosis by reading OBD-II fault codes to identify the misfiring cylinder(s), and check for a rough idle or hesitation matching that cylinder. 2) Tools/parts: OBD-II scanner, replacement ignition coil(s) matched to the affected cylinder(s), spark plug socket if plugs are inspected at the same time. 3) Disconnect the battery, remove the engine cover, unplug and unbolt the faulty coil(s), fit the new coil(s) and reconnect. 4) Clear the fault codes and verify with a test drive and a follow-up OBD-II scan that no new misfire codes appear. 5) This is a straightforward DIY job with basic tools; escalate to a workshop only if misfires persist after coil replacement, which points to a spark plug or wiring harness fault instead.
